title: Choosing a Function Model
short: Match data and situations to the right family of functions.

blocks.html: Real data rarely comes with a formula attached. Choosing a model means asking what kind of change you see, using everything from Exponential and Logarithmic Models, rational functions and polynomials.

Equal steps in $x$ with equal differences in $y$: linear. Equal second differences: quadratic. Equal ratios: exponential. Equal differences in $y$ when $x$ is multiplied by a constant: logarithmic. A quantity that shares out a fixed total (like time per worker) suggests a rational model.

Each family has its own signature. A line adds the slope for each unit step. A quadratic's differences grow by a constant amount, because its first differences are themselves linear. An exponential multiplies by $b$ for each unit step. A logarithm is the inverse of an exponential, so it adds a constant each time $x$ is multiplied by the base. Checking which pattern fits the data tells you the family.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Four families through $(1, 1)$ and $(2, 2)$: $f(x) = x$, $g(x) = \frac{x^2 + 2}{3}$, $h(x) = 2^{x - 1}$ and $p(x) = 1 + \log_2 x$. They agree on two points and disagree everywhere else.

blocks.title: A situation
blocks.q: A phone plan costs \$20 a month plus \$0.10 per text. Which model fits the monthly bill?
steps: Each extra text adds the same \$0.10.

blocks.html: Deciding from a picture of a few points. Many curves pass through any two points, as the visual shows. Compute differences and ratios, or think about the process that produced the data: a fixed percent change is exponential, a fixed amount is linear.
